claims.quote: Loss-of-function variants in SCN1A cause Dravet syndrome, the most common genetic developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (DEE).
emerging evidence suggests separate entities of SCN1A-related disorders due to gain-of-function variants.

Electrophysiological analysis showed a mixed gain-of-function effect with normal current density, a leftward (hyperpolarized) shift of steady-state inactivation, and slower inactivation kinetics leading to a prominent late sodium current.
Functional consequences of this variant lead to mixed loss and gain of function that is partially corrected by oxcarbazepine.

Both wild type and variant exhibited sensitivity to block by oxcarbazepine, partially correcting electrophysiological abnormalities of the SCN1A p.R1636Q variant.
Clinically, a single individual responded to treatment with oxcarbazepine.

claims.object_text: early onset DEE characterized by focal tonic seizures and additional seizure types starting in the first few weeks of life
claims.quote: All four individuals had an early onset DEE characterized by focal tonic seizures and additional seizure types starting in the first few weeks of life.

claims.object_text: neonatal onset epilepsy and absence of prominent movement disorder
claims.quote: The recurrent SCN1A p.R1636Q variant causes a clinical entity with a wider clinical spectrum than previously reported, characterized by neonatal onset epilepsy and absence of prominent movement disorder.

claims.object_text: earliest ages at onset among SCN1A-related epilepsies
claims.quote: Across 51 individuals with SCN1A-related epilepsies, those with the recurrent p.R1636Q variants had the earliest ages at onset.

claims.object_text: one of the most common causes of early onset SCN1A-related epilepsies
claims.quote: The recurrent p.R1636Q variant represents one of the most common causes of early onset SCN1A-related epilepsies with separate treatment and prognosis implications.
